In the *dāya* sacrifice, he throws a fuel-stick (*samidh*) into the fire. Then he offers clarified butter (*ājya*). He offers parched grains (*lāja*). These parched grains are indeed the form of the Ādityas. In that he offers with parched grains, he thereby gratifies the Ādityas. He makes this aspiration: "May this sacrificer [attain] long life; may he aspire for good offspring; may he aspire for companionship with his kinsmen; may he aspire for a higher sacrifice to the gods; may he aspire for the performance of further oblations; may he aspire for a celestial abode."

Through sacrifice and oblation, he prays for this; may the gods grant it to him, may they bestow it upon him. ... Tvaṣṭṛ begot you, O eightfold one; Tvaṣṭṛ has sent you forth as a bride. The meditation on the Goddess:
dark-complexioned, three-eyed, two-armed, and in a triple-bent posture.

With the right foot extended and the left foot drawn in, holding a blue lotus in the right hand and a *ṭaṅka* (or similar implement) in the left, with hands [in this manner], having worshipped the Supreme One thus, and having offered incense and lamps, one should present the food offering (*naivedya*) consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasa*), fruit, betel, and so forth. One should apply black fragrant unguents to the forehead and, with the *śikhā-mantra*, cause [the deity] to be placed upon the arm or the head.

Thereafter, one should cause the forms of Sadāśiva and the other deities to be offered; [one should] hold [the image] on the forehead and the neck with the *mūrtti*[-mantra], and with the *hṛdaya*[-mantra]... [one should place it] on the seat of the preceptor (*ācārya*). To the left of that, all [the attendants]—having been caused to ascend by the preceptor—[should be placed]. On both sides, dancers, male dancers, singers, and drummers, along with the fourfold performance of song and dance accompanied by musical instruments, having danced until the end, [they] should enter and perform [the ritual].

Thereafter, having established [the image] in its own place, having offered the *arghya*, and having presented the food offering (*naivedya*) along with fruits, one should worship it with services such as the water-sprinkling (*nīrājana*) and collyrium (*añjana*). Then, having bathed it with the products of the cow (*gavya-snāna*) and so forth, having praised it as before, having worn it for a day, having covered it with a white cloth and adorned it with very white jasmine flowers (*jāti-puṣpa*), one should present milk-rice (*pāyasa*).

Having offered incense and lamps, at the time of the procession, Pārvatī should proceed very slowly. There, having performed the procession as before with the sounding of the Vedas, dancing, singing, and so forth—and having performed everything such as the *nīrājanā* rite as before—one should enter the temple.

Having worshipped [her] with all ritual offerings and having circumambulated [the shrine], one should announce the protection against malevolent planets and the preservation of the remaining [community], as well as all public affairs, in that region. Without [offering] the *praṇapaka* (oblation) and the *guha-vya* (secret offering), one should cause her to enter the temple; then, having bathed her in her own place:

Having performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with [the mantra] *sna*... and the ritual for the dance (*nṛtta-vidhi*), immediately thereafter, on the tenth day, one should cause [the deity] to be bathed. On the eleventh day and night, having consecrated and adorned Indra... [and] having placed all the gods upon their celestial chariots (*vimāna*) and so forth, at the time of circumambulating the city, having adorned the northeast direction... with [offerings] raised upwards, one brings the entire Śiva seated in the middle of the celestial chariot from there. Having circumambulated the Lord, beginning as before and ending with Caṇḍeśa, one enters the temple; at that time, [one proceeds] to the front of the gateway (*gopura*) and the front of the sacrificial pit (*halmyā*).

Having prostrated... one should arrange for the viewing of the diversion. One should cause [the deity] to enter according to the prescribed rite; this is the procedure for the festival of the Goddess. Now follows the procedure for the festival of the devotees (*bhakta*). Having established the devotee (*bhakta*) either before Śiva or in a pavilion, and having performed the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) preceded by the bathing of both mobile and immobile icons (*bera*), one should perform the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) as previously described.

Having caused the devotee-icons or the devotees themselves to receive a full measure of perfumes and other offerings, and having presented them with saffron turbans, sacred threads, garlands, and so forth, and having offered praise through the forms of the devotees, the Preceptor (*ācārya*) should cause the devotees to receive powdered pigments for the night and offer betel leaves (*tāmbūla*) and other items.

Having circumambulated [the village] or the garland of villages and entered the temple, having established all [the deities] in their respective places, and having offered food offerings (naivedya), incense, lamps, and so forth, one should honor the teacher (ācārya) and those who know the songs of Śiva with garments, gold, and ornaments. Thus is the procedure for the festival of devotion (bhaktotsava).

The creation, maintenance, and destruction situated within the [three] locations, the binding of curiosity, and the secret application of camphor ointment; the vision of the dance in the fivefold splendor of grace; the characteristic of the installation of the living soul (jīvanyāsa); and [the placement] upon the middle of the trident, on the horn of the bull, in the middle of the footprint, in the belly of the peak, and on the head of the chariot.

In the nostrils, in the middle of the male organ, at the tip of the banner, in the place of the pitcher, and in the hand of the eight-formed [Lord], the wise declare that the *jīva* resides in the temple. In the case of fear from fire, it is on both sides; on the head of the *liṅga*, in the heart of the image, and so forth. In the form of devotion... the *jīvas* always reside indeed in the breasts of those made of metal.

The Liṅga, the Deśika, and the Nṛttarāja—[these] in the case of Somāskanda, or [others], are twelve in number. Kumāra has six threads, Śakti... nine, and Vighneśvara seven in number; there should be ten [of each] for the garments. Caṇḍeśa likewise has five, and the remaining deities should be nine.

One should install for the Ācārya the Liṅga-Gaurī and likewise Somāskanda; and one should support Śakti, Vighneśvara, [Kārttikeya], the flagstaff, Caṇḍeśvara, and Karṇa. There, having bowed down, one should perform the recitation (*japa*), singing, and the solstice-rite (*ayana*); and one should place the weapon (*astra*) and the Śakti on the right.

(1.2) ...and likewise at the internal equinox, there are two specific solstices. In Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo, the Sun moves with great speed... [the one] named Viṣṇuphalan... [the one] named Vikuṃ... the movement of the Sun for humans... sixty-eight [degrees] are declared as the face, because of the excess of merit in the poison. Sixteen *nāḍīs* are before the junction, and sixteen after the end of the conjunction.

In the present [era], in the region of Kṣetra, when the Nāḍī is stable from both sides... in the future, when Viṣṇu is present, likewise in Viśu; and when Viśve... has passed, during the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa). Upon the sighting of Rāhu, [or] in the increase of [the duration of] the day, one should perform the Sanandana and other rites at night, and also in those [other auspicious occasions].

And one should especially perform the festival of the deity (*devotsava*) right there for the sake of the subjects. Just as [the deity] is present here today... [so it should be done] until the end. Furthermore, at the time of the *saṅkrānti*, preceded by the ritual bathing (*asnāna*) and other rites as before, having consecrated the deity and adorned the primary *liṅga* and other icons with all ornaments, and having honored them with all musical instruments (*ātodya*).

...the essence... together with Bhakteśvara. Having performed a circumambulation of the village or the eastern [direction]... having performed the eye-ointment (*nīrāñjana*) and other rites as before at the site of Brahmā or in front of the bull, one should establish [the image] in its own place. Thus, when this is done, no monthly affliction shall exist for the kingdom.

Therefore, one should perform the festival with great effort (*tasmāt... prayatnena utsavaṃ samācaret*). This is the rule for the monthly festival (*māsotsavavidhi*). Now, regarding the fortnightly festival (*pakṣotsava*): on the eighth day, the fourteenth day, or the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)—when the digits [of the moon] have vanished—the Lord is present. [The days of] Dvyaṣṭacandra, Asinīvālī, Aṣṭacandra, and Arkā are [auspicious].

The first [tithi] begins immediately after the new moon (amāvāsyā). That [new moon], however, is to be known as purified by the *bhūtaśuddhi* ritual; even if it is a single moment, it is the new moon. If the first lunar day (*pratipad*) follows the new moon, the new moon must be divided into two parts for the rites pertaining to the gods (*daiva*) and the ancestors (*pitrya*). When the first lunar day overlaps with the preceding new moon during the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), [it is the one to be observed].

In the [signs] of Libra, Capricorn, Pisces, Virgo, Aries, and Gemini, as well as on the fourteenth day, the new moon, and the full moon, worship should always be performed with diligence. On the fourteenth day, there is the inexhaustible [merit] of the festival of the gods; on the fourteenth and the new moon, one should perform pilgrimage at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).

On the new moon day falling on a Monday, or on a Sunday, or on the seventh [tithi], or on the fourth [tithi] falling on a Tuesday—[on such occasions]... similar to... on the new moon with Monday... on that [day], one should commence Śivarātri. At night... one should perform the merit; one should celebrate the festival of the Goddess. By giving [gifts] on the new moon day, one obtains the fruit of a sacrifice, austerity, and charity... from death.

Now, regarding the New Moon festival (*amāvāsyotsava*): on the day of the new moon, having performed the great consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*) preceded by the bathing of the primary *liṅga* and other icons, and having adorned [the deity] with all ornaments and offered the great sacrificial oblation (*mahāhavis*), one should circumambulate the temple and so forth, accompanied by the goddess [Śakti], along with the umbrella, chowries, and other regalia—though without the sword and shield—and having spread [the ritual materials] in the designated place, and having performed the eye-anointing (*nīrāñjana*) and other rites as before, one shall attain a meritorious state through one’s own station. One who desires a son obtains a son; one who desires liberation attains liberation.

When it rains in due season... disease [is] of what form, as previously [stated] (as with a son)... on the new moon day (amāvāsya)... all... men... thus ends the ritual procedure for the New Moon festival (amāvāsyotsava-vidhiḥ). Now, regarding the Full Moon festival (paurṇamāsī-utsava): both Rākā and Anumati. On the full moon day... the leaf... by the month, Anumati is approved. ... The northern [fortnight] is called the "half-month" (pakṣa), and that which is named the fifteenth day is traditionally known as the Full Moon (paurṇamāsī). ... In the sixth house, [it is] desired... on the fifteenth... elephant... sin... in that house.

The path... that which [occurs] from every sunrise until sunset is renowned as "complete" (saṃpūrṇa), O sole god... O protector of the jewel... ...(l.6)...of all beings... between the two openings. Conjoined with Rudra... the fourteenth day and the full moon; the new moon is likewise conjoined with the Bhūtas; the Tīrtha... the great pair...

Then, on the full moon day, having consecrated the deity with the *pañcagavya* [five products of the cow] according to the ritual manual (*liṅga*), having adorned him with various wonderful ornaments, having offered the great sacrificial oblation (*mahāhavis*), and having presented seasonal fruits and the like along with betel leaf (*tāmbūla*), one should mount the deity upon a palanquin and lead him in circumambulation around the city or the temple.

"One should cause [the deity] to enter"—this is the procedure for the full-moon festival. Now follows the procedure for the constellation festival (*ṛkṣotsava*). At sunset, when the sun has set and the moon has risen, one should observe the constellation Śravaṇa at that very time, provided it has not yet departed. From the moment of its appearance until sunset, as long as it remains visible... having reached that day, one should observe it for half a watch (*yāma*).

One should perform the rite for that constellation; under Diti it would be Vāruṇa. [Under] Kumbhaka... Śiva... (l. 4) ...the man [attains his goal]. Under Apa... the ascent... under Saumya there would be a festival... (l. 5). Under Ārudrā there is all prosperity; the constellation Punarvasu [brings success]. Under Puṣya there is nourishment... (l. 5) ...under Pūrvaphalgunī there is good fortune.

One who is of a generous disposition obtains... (l. 6) ...but [there is] worship of Hara. ...Gain of speech through giving... the wish-fulfilling tree; having made a prostration... (l. 7) ...attainment in the void... acquisition in the Uttaras; in the Yuga... (l. 8) ...Aditi; in the Vāruṇa [asterism], goats and sheep in Proṣṭhapada... in the interval between those.

...by the sowing of anger (kopa), [one attains] the wind... the mantra. Therefore, with every effort, during these constellations (ṛkṣa)... at that limit... in the inheritance (dāya)... those [offerings] have gone... he obtains the gifts... in the Lakṣakye-s [places], even the thread-master (sūtraka) or the practitioner (sādhaka) who has been initiated (dīkṣita). ...all others... the sinner... the Vaiśyas... the people within [the kingdom].

...and even a widow [is successful] by means of a good boat and the wind... initiated (dīkṣita)... worship until night... and... and there, having beheld the Lord, having performed [the rite] once... to the Brāhmaṇas... according to one's ability... beyond that... without another. Without elaboration, as is fitting, having offered all the oblations... Soma...

...having performed the circumambulation of the village, beginning with the *nirāñjana* rite as previously described, one should cause [the image] to enter the temple... one should have it installed... there is no doubt. When the afflictions caused by the *grahas*, such as those of *mṛtyu* and *pūtanā*, arise, and when one is liberated from the [cycle of] existence, one rejoices for a double lifespan. One should worship on a Sunday... with offerings...

On Monday, [it is] auspicious and bestows happiness; on Tuesday, one shall obtain victory in battle. On Wednesday, [one obtains] desire; on Thursday, knowledge and mastery of the scriptures. On Friday, there is the acquisition of wealth and the destruction of untimely death. Having understood this, one should worship Śiva there with collyrium. Thus ends the ritual for the festival of the lunar mansions (*ṛkṣotsavavidhi*).

The expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for that [interruption] is said to be the reconnection of the channels (*nāḍī*). It is traditionally taught (*smṛta*) that the expiation is the reconnection of what has been lost again. One who measures [the time] with a moving particle would go to hell. For the sake of purifying one whose conduct has lapsed, the Guru should perform the expiation.

But for one who is intensely engaged in yoga, there is no fear of kings or thieves... O King, among those who follow the stages [of life], there is always... no sin... The expiation for celibate students (*brahmacārins*) and householders is... (l. 3)... these two have been proclaimed. For one who acts intentionally, the cessation [of the offense] for one who acts unintentionally is considered double. Double again from the *bhautika* [stage]... that same [expiation] applies to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika brahmacārin*). Even triple... (l. 4)

...the quality of one who stands [in that state]. When the sixteenth year has passed beyond [that period], for that bound child, one should prescribe half of the penance. For women and those afflicted by disease, half of the penance is declared. For one unable to perform it himself, the penance is doubled through another person. For one who is incapable, his son, brother, wife, and so forth, or his father and paternal kinsmen [shall act].

Having explained the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for one who has transgressed [the rules], one should, in an auspicious pavilion, construct a circular sacrificial pit (*vṛttakuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit in its center. Having prepared eight [vessels] possessing all the required characteristics—four of each kind, along with various types of offerings, accompanied by threads, lids, cloths, and *kūrca*-grass bundles, stainless and radiant—one should [invoke] the form of the Aghora-weapon with the mantra: *oṃ huṃ aghorāstramūrtte...*

...the Aghora meditation. [I meditate upon] Aghora, who has the luster of a water-laden cloud, possesses terrifying fangs and three eyes, wears serpents, is clad in red garments, and bears an axe, a *ḍamaru* drum, a sword, a shield, an arrow, and a trident... Having thus visualized him, one should worship with: *oṃ hūṃ aghorāstrāya namaḥ*.

Then, in the eastern foot-pot: *oṃ hāṃ śivāstrā...* | *oṃ śliṃ śi...mūrttaye namaḥ* | (l. 2) ... [with] hair like a mass of lightning, with the orb of the moon as his crest, and four sprout-like hands; joined with fire and flame, his... | endowed with twelve eyes, and holding a spear, a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.

Oṃ śliṃ, [worship] Śivāstra in the five-petaled lotus-vessel. Oṃ paṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Pāśupata weapon; Oṃ paṃ, obeisance to the form of the Pāśupata weapon. Having ascended the seat of the Praṇava, [one should meditate upon] the Yakṣa of great power, five-faced, three-eyed, with fangs formidable, emitting a loud roar, adorned with a garland of skulls, and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.

...and [bearing] the fear of the earth, adorned with serpent ornaments, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, and crushing the multitudes of obstacles; endowed with ten extremely fierce arms equipped with terrible weapons: a sword, a noose, a shield, an arrow, a skull-cup, and two excellent spears, [holding] barley-grains to the left; tawny-hued, with twin... and matted locks of hair—having meditated thus.

Oṃ Paṃ Pāsiṃ... Then, in the northern foot-vessel: Oṃ Śuṃ, obeisance to the terrifying weapon of Pratyaṅgirā; Oṃ Śuṃ, obeisance to the form of the weapon of Pratyaṅgirā. [She who has] a lion’s face... [with] a crest... resembling a dark cloud... endowed with... carrying... in her two true hands... the supreme ḍamaruka. Carrying [these] with her two right hands.

Having meditated thus: "Maṇyaśīrṣa... [endowed] with tears, meat, saliva, and falsehood; [endowed] with pearls... [and] jewels; [endowed] with... and speed; accompanied by a black antelope skin"—then, having offered worship to the faces and so forth, starting from the east and ending at the northeast, with the mantra: *Oṃ śuṃ, obeisance to the weapon of Pratyāṅgirā*.

The Śiva-knowledge beginning with the *Kāmika* and the *Tantra* born from the mouth of Him [Śiva], numbering five, etc., [should be recited]. In the various directions, they should recite the mantras beginning with Tatpuruṣa, numbering as many as there are directions. The study of the *Ṛg-veda* and so forth, and the recitation for peace (*śāntipāṭha*), should be performed without number, as prescribed in the *Pratiṣṭhā*. Immediately thereafter, when the time has arrived... [one] should [perform] one [rite].

Having worshipped the forms beginning with Kāmaghora, one should invoke the respective deities of the four sections (*kāṇḍa*) starting with Yamāntaka, and having worshipped them, they should offer honey-triad (*madhutraya*), sesame, *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth; or pure food, or milk-rice (*pāyasa*), or three heaps of honey and three fruits, or jaggery-juice with mustard seeds, or half of that, or one hundred and thirty times daily, both morning and evening, they should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) together with the *pūrṇā* offering.

At the end of the *svāhā*, O Blessed One, [recite] the word *sarvakṣobhān* again; perform the action (*kuruḥ*) joined with *kurvita* for each mantra at the intervals of ten. Thus, having established auspiciousness (*śivaṃ*) right there during many days or fortnights, one should go into the presence of the deity, announce the performance of the *homa* rite, apply protection with ashes (*bhasmarakṣā*), and pray for the destruction of misfortune (*duritakṣaya*). This is done over one, three, five, seven, nine, or twelve days.

Then, [the deities] are worshipped with the seven constellations of the birds (*pakṣini-sapta-nakṣatra*). Thus ends the ritual procedure for pacifying rites (*śāntikarma*). (Śāntihoma): ...As before, having entered the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and established [the deities] such as Vajra and others upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) accompanied by offerings of grain on the left... having placed [them], one should worship the firm seat (*sthira-āsana*) in the central jar (*kuṃbha*). In the central jar: *oṃ śiṃ pāśupatāstrāsanāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.

Oṃ śiṃ, homage to the form of the Pāśupata weapon, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Seated upon the throne of the Praṇava, possessing great strength, five-faced, ten-eared, with three eyes on each face, with a mouth terrifying to the Daityas, exceedingly fierce, difficult to conquer due to his loud roars, adorned with a garland of skulls, having the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, holding a staff, an axe, and the gesture of fearlessness, and endowed with serpent ornaments.

Having meditated thus: [the deity] possessing the brilliance of ten million suns, crushing the multitude of obstacles, endowed with ten fierce Bhairavas, and accompanied by [his] garment; holding in his right hands a sword, a bow, a great trident, a spear, and nooses; in his left hands a shield, arrows, skull-cups, a boon-granting gesture, and a lance; [and] likewise a [conch] shell and a headless corpse. Having meditated in this manner.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ śiṃ, obeisance to the Pāśupata weapon, huṃ phaṭ," and having fully honored [the deity] with all the services beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), and having performed the worship up to the stage of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga-pūjā*), one should worship the vases starting from the east and ending in the northeast, preceded by meditation, with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vajra; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śakti; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍa; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Khaḍga."

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the noose (pāśa). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the noose. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the goad (aṅkuśa). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the mace (gadā). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the trident (triśūla). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lotus (padma). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the discus (cakra). ... Having performed the oblation, one should worship Pracetas and Aṅgiras; this is the sacrificial offering. This is the procedure for the directional fire-offering (diśāhoma). ... at the forefront of the oblation...

Having placed [vessels] filled with water mixed with the eight substances beginning with *vajra* in the eight directions starting from the east—[vessels] covered with lids, wrapped in cloth, containing gold, jewels, medicinal herbs, and *gaṇḍa* flowers—in the eastern pavilion... [and so on]. In the center of that, one should worship the *aghorāstra* in the *vardhanī* vessel used for Śiva-initiation; or else, having placed the *śivakumbha* and the *vardhanī* in the center, one should worship the *aghorāstra* in that [vessel].

For the purpose of suppressing weapons such as the vajra and so forth on all sides: *oṃ aḥ ...astrāsanāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. *oṃ aḥ ...astramūrtaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. One should meditate [on him] as possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns, with the roar of clouds at the time of universal dissolution; his appearance is blazing, with a face [and forehead] marked by a laugh, and his eyebrows, beard, and hair are aflame. He wears a snake as a sacred thread and holds a trident, a sword, a spear, and a mallet.

Having meditated thus: "The four-armed [deity], of great body, adorned with serpent ornaments, the crusher of the arrogant gods, dānavas, and daityas," [one recites]: *sphura sphura prasphura prasphura ghora ghora tanurūpa caṭa caṭa pracaṭa pracaṭa kaha kaha vama vama bandhaya bandhaya ghāta*.

"...thus, *aghora-astāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. Having worshipped [the deity] with all the services beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), [one should visualize: 'Wearing black garments... [and] adorned on all limbs with suitable ornaments of pearls. Having meditated thus, one worships with: *oṃ hāṃ pratyaṅgirā-astāya hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ*."

Having worshipped [the deity] with the ritual services beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), and having performed the *nikṛtya* rite in the directions from the east to the northeast—or having prepared the *caru* according to the procedure prescribed for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*)—one should proceed up to the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) according to the method of the excellent enclosure. Having fully worshipped Maheśvarī in the center with *plakṣa* wood and other materials, along with products of the cow, sesame, *dūrvā* grass, milk, the three types of *caru*, and the three sweets (*madhuratraya*).

One should offer one hundred, one hundred, or fifty oblations for each of these sacrificial materials: the three fruits (*phalatraya*), the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*), *śrīparṇī* leaves, *śrīgaurī*, *gorocanā*, and so forth. Having offered the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścittāhuti*)—[whether] for the sake of the kingdom, the land, or [the disciple]—and having again offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should cause the Goddess to consume [the remains] for the pacification of that misfortune.

...having bathed the sacrificer (yajamāna) [in those waters], one should perform protection with the eight-fold ash (*aṣṭabhasmarakṣā*). Alternatively, as before, having worshipped Śiva together with his limbs (*sabrahmāṅga*) and his attendants (*sāṅga*) in either the perpetual fire (*nityāgni*) or the special fire (*viśeṣāgni*) in their midst, one should perform [the rite] for the sake of [the desired result]—such as a hundred, a thousand, or half [of that]—with sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) and other materials, using the mantras of Śiva together with his limbs, and so forth. ... *yanamaḥ*.

Having worshipped [the deity] with all the services beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), and having worshipped [it] with incense, perfumes, food offerings (*naivedya*), betel leaves (*tāmbūla*), and so forth; then, in the center of that, after performing the rites for the circular pit (*vṛttakuṇḍa*) and so on up to the concluding rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*); in the middle of the circle, as before, one should offer oblations of sacrificial wood (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), sesame seeds (*tila*), milk, flour-meal (*saktu*), *dūrvā* grass, the three sweets (*trimadhu*), the three fruits (*phalatraya*), and cooked rice (*caru*), along with the *brahmārdha* [portion], or half of that.

To remove those defects, having offered one hundred and eight oblations of the *astramantra* (the weapon-mantra), and having performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) according to the number of days prescribed for the rite of pacification (*śānti*), one should cause the recitation of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures, as well as the chanting of pacificatory texts, hymns, and *phaṭ*-mantras, to be performed from the *Kāmika-tantra* and other sources. After feeding the Brahmins, at the conclusion of the designated day, one should consecrate with the water from that jar; this is the *śāntihoma*.

The procedure for the *diśāhoma* sacrifice is for the purpose of expiation (*prāyaścitta*); another [procedure] beginning with the ritual bathing (*snāna*) and so forth may also occur. ... (l. 5) ... Having installed and fully worshipped the *liṅga*, the image (*bimba*), the water-pot (*ghaṭa*), and other items together with the altar (*vedikā*), one should place a single *śivāstra-kalaśa* in front of it. Then, having placed the *vajra*-kalaśas and others around it in the sequence starting from the east, (l. 6) and having worshipped the *śivāstra* in the central pot which is endowed with all splendors.

Oṃ haḥ, homage to the weapon of Śiva, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Oṃ haḥ, homage to the embodiment of the weapon of Śiva, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Having meditated thus: [upon the deity] who has four faces, whose hair blazes... with a radiance like a mass of lightning; whose head is the lunar disc, who possesses four sprout-like hands; who is joined with the fire of the world-destroyer, who is unbearable and of terrible prowess; who is endowed with twelve eyes and holds a spear, a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons. Thus, having meditated.

Oṃ haḥ, homage to the weapon of Śiva, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Having worshipped with all the services beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), and having worshipped with betel leaves and so forth in the jars... having prepared a circular, square, or sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila)... [offering] the sacrificial porridge (caru)... one should request permission; such is the procedure for the directional fire-offering (diśāhoma). Alternatively, in the center is the jar of Śiva, to its north the *vardhanī* vessel, and in the eastern direction the weapon of Śiva.

In the south is the Aghora-weapon; in the west... (l. 3) in the north is the Praty-aṅgirā-weapon—thus the limbs (*aṅga*). The syllable *oṃ*. Then the word "to the one clad in black" (*kṛṣṇavāsaseccha*). Then *cā...* in the face, and also "O Great-faced One" (*mahāvadana*), as well as "of the color of the Great Bhairava" (*mahābhairavivarṇāśca*), (l. 4) "all [the powers]... then the other... the word (*mantra*) for the destruction of all karma. Then: "cutting off eternally" (*cchedini nitya...*) and also "of all beings" (*sarvabhūtamanyapi*).

Then, for all beings... the supreme state (*padam uttare*). ... [regarding] previous obstacles, give... the state that is *ciddhiti*. Then, "cutting through all diseases" is the state of *nikṛnti*. Then, "devour all the wicked," *bhakṣa*, *bhakṣe*... one should practice. "O you with flaming tongues, O terrible one," *jvālājihve karāle*, and "O fang-bearing one"... after that is the state of *pratyaṅgira*. Then the state beginning with *oṃ namo*... the state that is...

...thus it is said... one should worship this mantra consisting of the Pratyāṅgirā [rite]: (l. 7) having worshipped the Supreme Goddess in the center of the assembly of all the cows, with the firm seat of the weapon-mantra of Pratyāṅgirā: *oṃ haḥ pratyāṅgirāstrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *oṃ haḥ pratyāṅgirāstramūrtaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. (l. 8)

[Visualize] the Lion, fierce, endowed with flames like fire, possessing three eyes, dark-hued, and withdrawn from sin; [him] bearing in both hands the Śukti... (line 1), Dūrvā grass, the three sweets, the three honeys... (line 2), and the Svardhani... (line 3); [and] the Lord of the Earth, the Protector of the Horse... (line 4). Having given the [appropriate] color... (line 4).

...the *liṅga* or the image... (l. 5)... for the number of days prescribed, one should perform all [the rites] in their entirety. ...(l. 6)... preceded by... with garments, gold, and other offerings, having performed the ritual... (l. 7)... together with the preceptor (*ācārya*), one should give the fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for those days, including food and clothing. ...(l. 8)... to the venerable Gurus. (p. 20a, l. 1) ...having worshipped the throne of Śiva (*śivāsana*). For the removal of its defects. Having performed the ceremonial bathing and the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma),
if another festival is held there instead, it will cause confusion for the village.
To prevent the recurrence of those defects, one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*).
Likewise, in this very context, one should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the pacification [of the defect]. (l.
4) ...the defect is indeed as stated in the *Yāmala*.
If there is the attainment of Vāmabhairava, the knot of the offering (bali) shall be destroyed.
If [the rite] has been performed through negligence regarding the bali offering, one should perform a *śānti*-oblation.
If it was performed while relying on a village boundary during a great bali ceremony, then there will be the destruction of the kingdom;
if that has occurred, one should perform the *śānti*.
Or when the site is powerful, or in front of a temple... (l.
6) ...it is recommended for the site of a deity's limb, especially for a surrounding enclosure;
likewise for a nearby site... a site with trees... (l. 7).

The other [type] is superior to that; its opposite is called the "Brahma-field" (*brahmakṣetra*). ... The intermediate [type], or rather that which is presided over by Him, is called the "inferior" (*hīna*).

They are to be distinguished by their specific characteristics... (p. 28b, l. 1)... and when one [of these] is stronger in a single case... Indeed, one who is capable should perform [the rite] elsewhere as a substitute (*kalpa*).
For those who have proceeded according to the non-substitute (*ananukalpa*), there is the *śāntihoma*... (l. 2).
...even if [the banner] is missing, it should be so for the recitation according to the number.
However, if the banner is missing at night, there is no fault... (l. 3)... if it is missing, then having performed the *mūrti-homa*, one should offer the *bali* at the end of the procession.
To the deities outside... (l. 4) in whichever direction [the deity] is outside...
that respective direction is indicated in the mantra... endowed with [these]. Just as... at the proper time, one should bring the offering (*bali*) to those respective deities. ...(l. 5)
Having entered, one is born [into the lineage]... then, having performed the *homa*, one should offer a *bali* characterized by food (*sānnaliṅga*).
(l. 6) Having made it firm, one should worship...
Having performed the *saṃhitā-homa*, immediately thereafter, one should remain established in that.
From this point forward, one should perform a circumambulation of that fallen sign...

When it has fallen, if the vessel has fallen, one should recite the Aghora mantra a hundred times. Having taken another [vessel] for the broken one, the materials for the *bali* offering... which have been prepared...

One should perform the pacifying rite that removes obstacles; having prepared the wood and other materials joined together with [the appropriate] mantras, one should carry them out according to the specific rites for each metal, and finally, after performing the concluding acts, one should perform the installation.

Having conquered [the obstacles] such as the breaking of the coverings while accompanied by worship at the *dhāma*, and having performed the rites beginning with the *pādya* according to the procedure, one should perform the festival (*utsava*). Having completed the festival rites, one should then perform the consecration (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) by means of the installation of the King of Weapons (*astrarāja*).
At the time of mounting [the vehicle] or when the *kula* has fallen... (l. 4)...

one should immediately perform [the rite]... when the *bera* has fallen, or as if it had fallen, [one should act] with two hands... or even after two nights or three nights, one should lead [the disciple] according to the sequence of the *cakra*. (l. 5)
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa), the rite of pacification (śānti), and the form-rite (mūrtti...); furthermore, the recitation of the thousandfold *ghorāveṇa* sound;
the offering of ordinary food (naivedya); and the festival (utsava).
Having tied the protective thread (kautuka), one should arrange the festival and so forth.
Or, in the case of one who is deficient in the head or other limbs, one should perform the rite according to the stated procedure for subsequent action (*anukarma*).
Therein, with the aforementioned image (*bera*), one should indeed perform the festival up to the point of rejoining (*sandhāna*).
O best of the twice-born, this should be performed daily by the preceptor (*deśika*) or [by others] for those who have ascended.

In the measurements of the womb-door and so forth, one must employ the correct proportions and not otherwise. Then, having fashioned the image (bera) according to the instructions for the subsequent ritual acts, one should thus perform the festival preceded by [the preliminary rites], as well as the festivals for the invocation of the deity and so forth.
In the case of the *liṅga*, there should be food; those initiated by Śiva [should perform] the ritual at the source of action. During the festival... the twice-born should return.
In the case of the image (*bera*), there is no fault at that time; for the pacification of the king, they shall proceed.
At that time, one should perform the *śānti*-homa as well as the *saṃhitā*-homa.
While performing these, it should be understood that for that purpose, even many villages are to be established.
One should recite five hundred times even when startled;
likewise, if the *bali* falls at that time, one should recite one hundred times.
If the *liṅga* or the carrier falls upon the ground...
The Guru should mutter the Ghoramantra one hundred times, and twice that number for the Śaṅkara and Astra mantras.
[This applies] during worship and sacrifice... [in cases of] various... (l. 5) ...of days, as well as for the incense, flowers, incense-sticks, and lamps.
One should perform [the rites] according to the prescribed rule with lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth. (l.

6) Even if the daily ritual (*āhnikakārya*) is omitted, or if the materials for the fire-oblation (*homadravya*) and the ointment (*vilepana*) are missing, or if the boat has been extinguished, or even if Śiva is accompanied by [his consort] or is otherwise absent, [the rite should still be performed]. (l. 7)
If [he] is deprived [of these], he should perform the mounting of a chariot;
at the time of departure, [reciting] "Bhago bhuvodbhuve...
[he becomes] fit for the vehicle, and fit for the action of the shoulder-yoke of Indra’s chariot.
If a quarrel should arise at the time of viewing the diversion,
one should then perform a *śānti-homa* or an *aghora-homa*. For those who are deficient, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is as previously stated.

In the case of the bathing at the end of the vehicle (*yānāntasnapanam*), when the *śāntihoma* has been omitted, O Deva... one should perform the *śāntihoma* for the sake of attaining presence (*sannidhi*). Or, once the vehicle of the deity (*devayāna*) has been set in motion by one who is empowered (*adhiṣṭhita*), one should perform the moving bath (*carāsnapanam*).
Having then performed the *śāntihoma*, they [the officiants] should carry it out with those [materials].
When the festival of the Dancing Form (*nṛttamūrti*) is deficient, one should perform it for that purpose. Afterwards, at the desired time, one should perform the circumambulation of Naṭeśa.
In the event of the interruption of the sacrificial procession (*yātrādāna*) during the evening rites... (l.
7) ...if there is a deficiency [in the ritual], there shall be a sacrifice for the king (*nṛpyāyajaya*).
Having then performed a propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*), [the rite proceeds] when the hunt (*mṛgayā*) is deficient. (l. 8)
If, subsequently, when the rite for the *tīrtha* has been performed,
there should be a deficiency, then in due order one should perform a *śānti-homa*;
or, in the case of a deficiency, one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa*.
When this raising of the flag at Kautukatīrtha takes place, one should perform the auspicious bath (*kautuka-snāna*)... (l. 2) ...there would be affliction by disease.
There should be a propitiatory fire-oblation (*śānti-homa*), O Aṅgiras, and there should be a *saṃhitā*-offering at the Liṅga.
For one who has been deprived [of merit] at a great *tīrtha*, [it becomes] fruitless...
when that [merit], such as the previous *nandī* and so forth, exists otherwise in the present.
Then, for the sake of pacifying this fault, one should perform a *śānti-homa*.
...(l.4) ...the *saṃhitā-homa* sacrifice was performed; there shall be fear for the king.
Having released Mitra and the others from that very place and then outside, I have performed the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) by which the region... (l.5)... [is purified].

And indeed, there is the sprinkling for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhaprokṣaṇa*). Having abandoned the site where death has occurred or where a birth has taken place, one should prepare a suitable [place]. In the middle of the sacrificial ground (*yāgasthala*), there should be an application of plaster;
there, one should sequentially arrange the auspicious day and the sprinkling with *gavya* (cow-products).
And at the end, having performed the communal feast for the Śaivas... (l. 7)... one should sprinkle [the area]... it should be so.
One should perform the *śānti* oblation when there is a pavilion; and in the case of a pavilion for the image, one should perform the *śānti* oblation again and again. (l. 8)
One should perform the sprinkling at the end. For the gods, there is the bathing, the propitiatory rite (*śānti*), and the fire-oblation (*homa*).

One should sprinkle with cow-products (*gavya*)... [p.31a, l.1] ...with waterless [substances]. If the interior of the hall is barren, one should perform the bathing and offer oblations in the ten directions according to the prescribed method.
When death or similar events occur in places such as cremation grounds,
one should perform the rite of encircling with fire (paryagnikaraṇa),
and finally carry out either the offering to the directions (diśāhoma) or the offering to the deity’s form (mūrtihoma).
If [the obstacle] is external, one should first perform a *śānti-homa*.
In this very manner, there may occur here [consequences] such as the death of the *hotṛ* priest and so forth;
from that day onwards, there may arise burning, cutting, and other such calamities.
The results for when one is "bitten" by rats and other such creatures are stated here:

in the corner (koṇa), there is the increase of enjoyment; at the end (prānta), it is proclaimed as inauspicious; from the son (putra) and the middle of the row (paṅktimadhya), [the result] is in the middle of the hope of the period (daśā).
...and having made the treatise possess excessive qualities...
the fault has been fully described; no other is mentioned.
In this very same way... and having performed the ritual for bathing... (l. 5)
Having recited the Aghora mantra one thousand times, one should cause the garments of those bitten to be given away.
Or else, for the sake of Śiva, for those who have been initiated and who carry [the burden] upon their hands,
one should perform the Saṃhitā-homa or then recite the Aghora mantra.
And once [the disciple] has been initiated by Rudra and the others, having entered... (l.

7), one should sprinkle him with the *astra*[-mantra] and recite the mantra. When that [initiation] has been performed upon the water-pot (*kuṃbha*) and so forth, one should place another [disciple] therein; however, at the time of entry, it must be preceded by the *saṃhitā-homa*.
Having inspected the smearing with cow dung...
[the vessels] for birth-impurity and death-impurity, and those situated therein... [the smearing with] cow dung...
(p.31b, l.1)... from the great milking, may there be for me peace; one should perform the *śānti-homa* sacrifice.

If [the disciple] is of a suitable nature, then the previously mentioned finger-ring mantra should be bestowed. Having completed the hundred-fold recitation of the Aghora mantra, one should receive from the Guru those [mantras] as prescribed. By a single teacher, that which resides in a single temple should be performed using gold.

The karma performed by another... that [karma] would be cut off. The teacher... [is] the protector. (l. 4) ...the fetching of water and so forth, the preparation of perfumes, flowers, incense, and the like;
the lighting of lamps, the offering of food (naivedya), the accomplishment of the essence, the constant accumulation for the noble ones; all this is fuel. (l. 5)

...the worship of the *liṅga* and so forth, the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*), and the performance of various rites at their respective times— he performs them all as one. Regarding the rule that "the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites must be performed by the teacher according to their established times," this is well said.
The son or grandson of this teacher...
those who desired his instruction...
(l. 7) ...a Brāhmaṇa born in a lineage of true Śaivas... the twenty-third.
Regarding the touching of cow dung... (p.32a, l.1)... it is proclaimed that [the sin] is *niṣkala*.
For *caṇḍa*... (l.2)... one should perform the expiation (*niṣkṛti*).
...(l.3)... the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). In the kitchen... (l.4)... in the pavilion of the site (*sthānamaṇḍapa*) and so forth. ...(l.5)
...in the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) and half in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the image and so forth... (l. 6) ...the form is likewise made of gold.
There is a fire-offering for peace (*śāntihoma*) and the *Saṃhitā*... (l. 7) ...as prescribed for the pavilion... (p. 32b, l.
1) ...the hair, those [substances] such as perfume (*gandha*)... Rudraka and Maddāsya, one’s own [offering]...

But by those endowed with knowledge, even through *sāman*... whatever has been done... one should perform pacification (*śānti*) therein. Even the fault of the performer [is removed], and the fruit indeed... one should abandon that which is established by the *astra* [mantra] and must be performed. Otherwise...
for the cessation of the fault, only that which is established by the scripture is the prior limit. Then... it is fully understood from the very foot of the ritual action (*kriyāpāda*).
The procedure for expiation... from the sixtieth [chapter]...
(p.33a, l.1, blank) (p.32b, l.1)...in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

Having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) in four ways, and having installed the form (*mūrti*), [one recites]: *Oṃ hāṃ... Oṃ hāṃ lūṃ kṣmā-mūrtaye namaḥ* in the primary sacrificial pit (*pradhānakuṇḍa*). Having divided that [pit] into nine parts, in those [sections] starting from the east: *Oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya namaḥ*; *Oṃ heṃ... namaḥ*. Having offered three oblations (*āhuti*) with *Oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya svāhā*, and having taken [the fire] in a shallow dish (*śarāvapātra*), one places it in the eastern square pit (*caturaśrakuṇḍa*) [with]: *Oṃ hrīṃ āhvanīyāgnaye namaḥ... mūrtaye namaḥ*.
He has one face and three eyes, three girdles, and three feet;
he holds a rosary and a trident in his right hands.
He is red in color, seated comfortably, and enveloped by a yellow garment.
One should meditate upon the Āhavanīya fire in the center of the eastern pit.

Having established [the deity] in that same manner, [one should worship] Brahmā and the others among the attendants. Having performed the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*), [one recites]: *oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*, *oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣavaktrāya namaḥ*. [He is] in yellow garments... [to him] who has the moon as his crest. *oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*.

Having thus performed the worship and effected the union of the fire from the mouth of Śiva with [the external] fire, [one offers oblations]: "Oṃ, obeisance to the form of Tatpuruṣa... (p. 34a, l. 1). "Oṃ hāṃ lūṃ, obeisance to Śarva, the lord of the Kṣmā-form, who possesses four faces and eight arms, and is clothed in yellow garments. (l. 2) ... "Oṃ lūṃ, obeisance to Śarva, the lord of the Kṣmā-form. "Oṃ huṃ, svāhā to the Āhavanīya fire, to the face of Tatpuruṣa. "Oṃ heṃ, svāhā to the face of Tatpuruṣa. (l. 3) ... "To the face of Tatpuruṣa, huṃ phaṭ svāhā"—this is the kindling (*dīpana*). "Oṃ heṃ, svāhā to the face of Tatpuruṣa."

Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to the fire to be invoked. ... [The] clarified butter, wheat, and other substances that have been prepared, as well as the Śivāstra, bestow the fruit of all creation. Having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) on the right side—[reciting]: "Oṃ kṣuṃ, obeisance to the form of the sacrificer (*yajamāna-mūrti*); Oṃ hāṃ ślūṃ, obeisance to the form of the sacrificer"—and on the right side: "Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to the seat of Aghora; Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to the form of Aghora; Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to Aghora. Having thus worshipped...

...having given [the oblation]... and having taken it in a shallow vessel (*śarāva*), one should place it in the southern fire-pit (*dakṣiṇakuṇḍa*)... *Oṃ*... (l.8)... gold and so forth, and the four tongues in the right face. Suprabha... (p.34,b, l.1)... and likewise a ladle (*sruk*) and a vessel of ghee (*ghṛtapātra*).
A lance (*tomara*) and an axe (*paraśu*) in the left [hands]. Visualizing him as seated upon a goat-vehicle (*ajavāhana*) as the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, one should worship in the southern fire-pit. (l.2)

...for the sake of protecting against fire, having worshipped with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*) beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), and having performed the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)—having worshipped with "Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to the one whose form is non-terrible (*aghoramūrti*); Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to Aghora"—the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
[He] holds a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a shield (*kheṭa*), a skull-bowl (*kapāla*), and a noose (*pāśa*) in his left hands, and an axe (*paraśu*) and a trident (*triśūla*) [in his right].
And one should meditate upon Aghora, who holds a sword and a staff, whose face is terrifyingly distorted, and who is adorned with serpents and other ornaments.

Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the one whose form is Aghora (Aghoramūrtaye). Having performed [this], [one recites]: Oṃ hāṃ śūṃ, obeisance to the form of the sacrificer (Yajamānamūrtaye). Having worshipped thus with "Oṃ hāṃ śūṃ, obeisance to the form of the sacrificer," [one offers oblations with]: Oṃ hrīṃ... svāhā; Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to the heart of Aghora (Aghorahṛdayāya); and Oṃ hūṃ, huṃ phaṭ to the heart of Aghora. Having offered one hundred oblations, and having offered one hundred oblations with "Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the Southern Fire (Dakṣiṇāgnaye)," [one offers] fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood and so forth, along with oblations of food and clarified butter, for the sake of pacifying Aghora.

...having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the four steps, in the *kuṇḍa*... [in the heart] *oṃ hāṃ sūṃ*, obeisance to Indumūrti... (l. 2)... obeisance. In the northern *pradhānakuṇḍa*: *oṃ hiṃ*, obeisance to Vāmadeva-guhya. Having worshipped thus and offered three oblations (*āhuti*), one should take the fire into a shallow dish (*śarāva*). In the northern *padmakuṇḍa*: ...obeisance to Kevalāgni. Having thus fully worshipped the seat-form (*āsana-mūrti*) and the root-form (*mūla-mūrti*), the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
Having two eyes and two arms, joined with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
he is clothed in white garments and adorned with white jewels.
...having meditated upon the solitary fire in the center of the sacrificial pit and in the north...

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kevalāgni," and having fully worshipped [the deity] for the protection of the fire with all ritual offerings (*upacāra*), and having performed the rites up to the point of consecration (*saṃskāra*), one should meditate as follows: "Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the secret Vāmadeva; Oṃ hiṃ, to the secret Vāmadeva, huṃ phaṭ. [One should offer] a garland, clothing, and a sacred thread (*upavīta*). Having meditated on [him] as having a prominent nose, a red turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), and being equipped with a sword and a shield.

...Oṃ hāṃ sūṃ... *namaḥ* to the seat of the form (*mūrtyāsana*). [The] meditation (*dhyāna*): [He is] seated in a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) that is both lunar and gentle... (l. 8)... endowed with [all attributes]. Oṃ hāṃ sūṃ, *namaḥ* to Mahādeva, the lord of the lunar form (*indumūrti-adhipati*). Oṃ hāṃ sūṃ, *namaḥ* to the lunar form (*indumūrti*). Having thus worshipped (p. 35b, l. 1)... *svāhā*. Oṃ hiṃ, *svāhā* to the secret [aspect] of Vāmadeva. Thus is the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Oṃ hiṃ, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā* to the secret [aspect] of Vāmadeva. Thus is the illumination (*dīpana*). Oṃ hiṃ... one hundred oblations (*āhuti*). Oṃ hrīṃ, *svāhā* to the solitary fire (*kevalāgni*). Thus [one offers] one hundred... and the weapon-mantra (*astra*).

Having thus offered one hundred oblations, and having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)—beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa* and ending with *catuṣpadha*—in the *bilva*... form *kuṇḍa*, [one should offer] obeisance to Rudra, the presiding deity of the [principal] form (*mūrti*). In the western *pradhāna-kuṇḍa*, [one should say]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta-mūrti. Having worshipped [him] with *āvāhana* and the other rites, and having taken [the fire] and placed it in the western *kuṇḍa*, having kindled it, [one says]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Gārhapatya."

Meditation on Gārhapatya: One should meditate upon Gārhapatya as having red limbs, holding a *sruc* and a *sruva* in his two upper hands, adorned with ornaments of pearls, endowed with seven tongues of flame, possessing one face, and bearing matted hair (*jaṭā*). Mounted upon a horse, one should worship him with "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Gārhapatya. Then, for the protection of the fire, having likewise placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*) in the enclosures starting from the east, [one worships] with "Obeisance to the Form (*mūrti*) of the *sruc*, *sruva*, and clarified butter (*ājya*). Meditation on the [Form]:
Richly adorned with white *sruc*, incense, and ornaments, wearing a white turban and white garments.

In the north, having worshipped with "Oṃ Haṃ, obeisance to the Sadyojāta form," [the deity] who possesses a moon upon his head, has the appearance of a youth, and holds a water-pot in his hand; then, having joined the fire of Śiva’s mouth with the mouths of Śiva, [one worships] with "Oṃ Hāṃ... obeisance to Bhava.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:

Having worshipped the one whose essence is the form of four arms, adorned with all ornaments, who is like the dawn preceding the sacrifice, and who is the purifier of the god of love (Makaraketana): *oṃ haṃ svāhā to Sadyojāta and Bārhapatya*; *oṃ haṃ svāhā to the form of Sadyojāta*. Thus is the libation (*tarpaṇa*).

Oṃ haṃ sadyojātamūrttaye huṃ phaṭ... Oṃ haṃ sadyojātamūrttaye svāhā. Having thus offered a hundred oblations with [the mantra] "Oṃ hrīṃ gārhapatyāgnaye svāhā," and having offered clarified butter, mung-bean products, and other substances, [he places] the grain... in the direction of Agni (the southeast).

...having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the fourfold [rite], in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of fire (*vahnimūrti*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lord of the form of fire... (l. 7); and with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the heart (*hṛdaya*)," and having offered three oblations (*āhuti*); having taken [the materials] into the vessel; the meditation on the Fire (*agni*)—four-armed, three-eyed, one-faced, and wearing matted locks.

[He holds] a trident, an axe, and likewise the gestures of fearlessness and the granting of boons. (p.36b, l.1) ... *Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Vṛddhāgni*. Having thus invoked [the deity], for the protection of the fire, one should encircle the first girdle starting from the east... having performed the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, [one places them] in the center of the *kuṇḍa*. *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Heart*. The visualization (*dhyāna*):
The heart is as radiant as the moon, endowed with the gestures of the boon and fearlessness.

...(l. 3)... *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the heart.* Having meditated thus and having joined the fire of Śiva’s mouth with the mouth of Śiva, [one says]: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of the form of Fire*. (l. 4)... the face above the shape of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), blazing, the foot-water... *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Fire*. (l. 5)... *Salutation to Paśupati, the lord of the form of Fire.* Having worshipped thus: *Oṃ hāṃ... svāhā to Vṛddha and Agni*. *Oṃ hāṃ*...

"Oṃ *hṛdayāya svāhā*"—this is the libation (*tarpaṇa*). "Oṃ *hāṃ hṛdayāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*"—this is the kindling (*dīpana*). "Oṃ *hāṃ hṛdayāya svāhā*"—[recite] one hundred times. Having offered oblations of *pratyaṅgirā* one hundred times with "Oṃ *hrūṃ vṛddhāgnaye svāhā*", and having offered sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) from the *nyagrodha* tree and so forth, along with rice, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and other substances.

There shall be an increase in progeny. In the northeast, having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa* and ending with the fourfold [rites] in an octagonal fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should worship in one's own heart: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Space-form (*vyomamūrti*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the lord of the Space-form. Having worshipped thus in the primary pit in the northeast with "Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the Head," and having offered three oblations (*āhuti*), one should collect the fire in a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), place it in the northeastern pit, and kindle it. Then: "Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the Common Fire (*sāmānyāgni*). The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:

One should place [the deity] with two faces, the Veda-peak, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the spear (*śakti*), the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), and the spoon (*sruva*), with the boon-granting gesture (*varada*) on the left; one should then install the general form of the fire-god (*agni*) in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the directions.

...Having worshipped with "Obeisance to the Universal Fire" (*sāmānyāgnaye namaḥ*), and having established [the guardians] in pairs upon the tiers (*mekhalā*) starting from the east for the protection of the fire, and having performed the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should meditate thus within the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*): "Oṃ Hīṃ, obeisance to the Head. The head, resembling a conch-shell, [granting] fearlessness... Having meditated thus and worshipped, and having offered the oblation (*homa*) that joins the fire of Śiva’s mouth with the mouth of Śiva, [one recites]: "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the Space-form (*vyomamūrti*). The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:

Having meditated [on him] as four-armed and four-faced, holding a trident, a *ḍamaruka* drum, a conch, and a *khaḍvāṅga*, with the luster of a *kunda* flower or snow; having thus meditated, and having meditated [further] with "Obeisance to the form of the crest (*śikhāmūrti*)", and having worshipped, one effects the union of the face of Śiva and the fire-face. Then: *oṃ hāṃ...* [and so on], [he is] the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), crowned, lotus-handed, adorned, ruddy... [and] wise.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Arkamūrti. ... hrūṃ ... [svāhā]. Oṃ huṃ, svāhā to the Śikhā; thus is the libation (tarpaṇa). Oṃ hūṃ, vauṣaṭ to the Śikhā. ... svāhā to that which is in the southeast. Having thus offered the *prata...* and the Śiva-Gāyatrī mantra, [one offers] oblations of fuel-sticks from the Plakṣa tree and so forth, along with rice and clarified butter. Śālyā... (line 5).

...having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the four steps, in the *rūpakuṇḍa*...(l. 6)... [reciting] "Oṃ hāṃ yuṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the Vāyumūrti... In the *pradhānakuṇḍa*, in the quarter of Vāyu, having offered [the oblation] "Oṃ" ...(l. 7)... and having taken a leaf from a bowl made of *aśvattha* wood and so forth, and having kindled it, [reciting] "Oṃ hruṃ" ...(l. 8)...

...having two nostrils; a quadrangle... [the] sacrificial ladle (*sruk* and *sruva*) and the rosary... (p. 38a, l. 1) ...homage to Abhimāna, the presiding deity of the Form (*mūrti*). Having thus worshipped, and having offered oblations with substances and so forth to the common fire (*sāmānyāgni*) with "Oṃ... svāhā" (l. 2), and having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the fourfold path (l. 3).

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Sun-form (Arka-mūrti). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of the Sun-form. ... (l. 4) ... salutation to the crest-lock (śikhā). Having thus worshipped and offered three oblations, [one should] kindle the fire in a shallow vessel (śarāva-pātra). ... (l. 5) ... Meditation: Three-eyed, five-faced, red-bodied... constantly... [holding] nooses, lotuses, and wheels.

...and likewise on the left [side]. On the right, [in] Hiraṇyakanaka... (l. 7)... Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ ...obeisance to Agnimūrti. Having thus worshipped, for the protection of the fire, one should place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*) upon the girdles starting from the east... (l. 8)... in the center of the *kuṇḍa*: Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Śikhā. The visualization (*dhyāna*): the crest (*śikhā*) of the color of vermilion... (p. 38b, l. 1) (damaged) (p. 39a, l. 1).
